title: What Actually Makes Leadership Spiritual
subtitle: Spiritual leadership is not the same thing as competent leadership in a Christian building, and the difference is the one most pastors never stop to measure.

sections.title: Competence Wearing the Clothes of the Spirit
sections.body:
A man can run a church for years on pure competence and never once depend on God. I have done it. I have planned the service, written the sermon, managed the staff, grown the budget, and gone home satisfied, and somewhere in all that motion the Spirit became optional and I did not notice the day He left the room.

This is the great deception of the work. Spiritual leadership and skilled leadership look identical from the outside. Both fill the calendar. Both produce results. Both draw the praise of good people who cannot see the difference because the difference is invisible. The crowd cannot tell whether the power running the machine is the Holy Spirit or your own talent, because the machine runs either way, for a while.

Not all church work is spiritual work. Some of it is religious activity powered by a gifted man who learned long ago that he does not strictly need God to pull it off. The tragedy is not that such a man fails. The tragedy is that he succeeds, and calls it ministry, and never finds out what he traded away.

The building is full. The leader is empty. No one can see the gap but God.

sections.title: Leadership That Comes From Somewhere Other Than You
sections.body:
What makes leadership spiritual is not the subject matter. It is the source.

A man can teach the Bible from his own cleverness. He can counsel the grieving out of his own warmth. He can cast vision from his own ambition and dress all three in the language of God. The words are right. The source is wrong. Spiritual leadership is leadership that draws its life from a life outside itself, from the actual present help of God, sought in prayer, received in dependence, and not from the leader's own considerable reserves.

This is why Jesus said apart from Him we can do nothing, and meant it as a description and not a threat. Not less. Nothing. Whatever a branch produces while severed from the vine is not fruit. It may look like fruit. It may even taste like it for a season. But it is wax, and the heat of any real trial melts it.

The question is never how much you accomplished. The question is who was the source of it. Those are not the same question, and we keep answering the easier one.

sections.title: How to Tell Which Kind You Have Become
sections.body:
There is a test, and it is brutal, and it is reliable.

Watch what happens in you when the work goes badly. When the numbers fall, when the criticism comes, when the season is dry and nothing you do seems to land. A competent leader running on his own steam panics in that season, because his own steam is all he has and it is failing. A spiritual leader has somewhere else to go, and goes there, and is steadied by a hand that is not his own. The dry season exposes the source. It always has.

Watch, too, what feeds your soul. If your private walk with God survives only as long as it produces public material, you are not a spiritual leader. You are a man mining his own devotion for content. The prayer that exists to fuel the sermon is not prayer. It is preparation wearing prayer's coat.

Watch where you turn first when you are afraid. To the phone, or to the throne. The answer is the diagnosis. We already know what ours is.

sections.title: Why the Spiritual Kind Is Harder and Slower
sections.body:
Here is why most of us drift toward competence. It is easier.

Dependence is humiliating. It means starting the day on your knees with empty hands, admitting that the gift God gave you is not enough, that the experience you have accumulated cannot carry the weight, that you need Him today as much as you did the first day. Competence flatters. Dependence exposes. And the longer a man does this work, the more competent he becomes, and the more competence offers to spare him the daily humiliation of needing God.

So we take the offer. Not in a dramatic act of unbelief, but in a thousand small efficiencies, each one a place where we decided we could handle this part without asking. The prayer gets shorter because the skill got longer. The dependence thins because the competence thickened. And one day a man realizes he has built an entire ministry he no longer prays about, because he no longer feels he has to.

The spiritual kind costs you your self-sufficiency. That is the whole price. That is why so few pay it.

sections.title: Coming Back to the Vine
sections.body:
The good news is that the way back is short, because the vine never moved.

You do not have to rebuild your devotion from scratch. You have to stop pretending you can do this without Him and start the day again with empty hands. That is repentance for a leader, and it is not a one-time event. It is the daily decision to be a branch and not a generator, to receive rather than to manufacture, to lead from a life you did not produce.

Moses said it plainly to God in the wilderness. If your presence does not go with us, do not send us up from here. He had the people, the calling, the track record, the staff that split a sea. And he said none of it was worth carrying one mile without the presence of God. That is a spiritual leader. He would rather have nothing with God than everything without Him.

Measure yourself against that sentence. Not the size of the thing you are leading. Whether you would still want it if His presence were not in it. That answer is your ministry, and only you and God know it.
